title: Fuel Tax (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2006

divisions.question: Debate resumed. Ron Boswell We are debating the [Fuel Tax Bill 2006](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R2518) today, which will bring into effect legislation that will remove excise from many fuels. It is designed to simplify the way tax credits for fuels are administered. It replaces and adds to the Energy Grants (Credits) Scheme. And what it effectively does is provide a mechanism to allow a greater number of businesses to claim back the fuel tax that has already been paid. There are a number of aspects of this bill which I am happy to commend. These include the provision to allow rebates on tax paid to all off-road fuel users. In effect, this allows fuel excise exemption for every farmer that has a petrol pump auger or for any petrol that is used off-road. That is going to be a great benefit to many regional and rural users of petrol on farms. I see Senator Scullion in the chamber today. He will be rejoicing on behalf of the fishing community, because it will also exempt all petrol used in outboard motors. As a former fisherman, and a very successful one at that, he knows it will make a huge difference to the fishing industry. This bill removes about $800 million in extra fuel tax credits to business right across Australia, whether it be fishing, forestry, mining or primary producers. This means any petrol or fuel that is used in those industries will have an excise exemption, and that is a big plus. It means a business will be able to operate more effectively as the level of tax for these businesses is being reduced. One aspect of the bill is to centralise a system of fuel tax credits through the Australian Taxation Office, rather than through a number of different departments and schemes as is currently the case. speeches.speaker: Eric Abetz
speeches.brief: The Fuel Tax Bill 2006 and its companion bill replace existing fuel tax concessions with a single fuel tax credit system from 1 July 2006, lowering compliance costs and reducing tax on business. Large fuel users receiving over $3 million per year in credits must join the Greenhouse Challenge Plus Programme, and the system will be fully implemented by 1 July 2012.

speeches.speaker: John Hogg
speeches.brief: A committee report on the Fuel Tax Bill 2006 and a related bill, along with the Hansard record and documents, was presented to the President and authorised for publication and printing.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Fuel Tax Bill 2006 would harm the biofuels industry and rural communities, and moved an amendment calling for a review in 2009 of the proposed excise on biofuels.

speeches.speaker: Ron Boswell
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Fuel Tax Bill 2006 would simplify fuel tax credits and provide excise exemptions for off-road business users like farmers and fishers, but expressed concern that treating biodiesel rebates as excise rather than a production subsidy would disincentivise its use and harm the biofuels industry. He also noted the removal of the Fuel Sales Grants Scheme and a two-year transitional period for claiming rebates.

speeches.speaker: Lyn Allison
speeches.brief: Senator Allison moved three amendments to the Fuel Tax Bill 2006, arguing that the bill would make biodiesel more expensive than diesel and disadvantage the fledgling biofuels industry, and provided examples showing that without the amendments, a B49 biodiesel blend would cost $1.03 per litre in 2007 compared to diesel at 97.8 cents, whereas her amendment would keep it at 85 cents.

speeches.speaker: Richard Colbeck
speeches.brief: The government moved the Fuel Tax Bill 2006 and the Fuel Tax (Consequential and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2006 for a third reading, arguing there is no effective excise on biodiesel and that any disadvantage to biodiesel stems from production costs, not the bill. The bill was passed without amendment.
